topic: Research: Google ADK + A2A Protocol: Cross-Framework Agent Interoperability Guide

key_points: Shows a practical path for converting a standalone ADK agent with MCP tooling into an A2A-compatible service.
Explains AgentSkill and AgentCard as the public discovery identity for an agent.
Uses an AgentTaskManager / AgentExecutor bridge to translate A2A requests into ADK runner execution.
Demonstrates an orchestrator agent that discovers A2A agent cards and calls remote agents as tools.
Beginner-friendly build path that combines MCP, ADK, Cloud Run, and A2A in one currency-agent example.
Frames MCP as the agent-to-tool layer, ADK as the agent-building and orchestration layer, and A2A as the agent-to-agent communication layer.
Includes cloud deployment and authentication steps, which makes it useful for readers moving beyond local demos.
Covers exposing an ADK-built currency agent as an A2A server and testing it with an A2A client.
Enterprise-oriented explanation of A2A as a standardized communication layer for cross-vendor agent discovery, authentication, and collaboration.
Highlights protocol mechanics including JSON-RPC 2.0, HTTP/HTTPS, Server-Sent Events, Agent Cards, task lifecycle states, messages, and artifacts.
Strong comparison between A2A and MCP: A2A coordinates autonomous agents while MCP connects an agent to tools and context.
Raises production-readiness caveats: partnerships do not always prove production deployments, so teams should start with proof-of-concept validation.
Provides a concrete cross-framework example connecting Microsoft Agent Framework and Google ADK through A2A.
Emphasizes the well-known agent metadata endpoint as the discovery contract.
Useful angle for developers who need best-of-breed systems instead of a single-framework architecture.
Identifies next-step concerns such as authentication, streaming responses, and multi-agent orchestration.
Hands-on tutorial that turns ADK sub-agents into standalone A2A applications.
Calls out ADK's to_a2a() helper as a fast way to wrap an existing ADK agent as an A2A app.
Uses multiple small agents to explain why A2A is useful for distributed agent systems and separation of concerns.
Good practical complement to official docs because it shows a compact multi-service developer workflow.

stats.fact: A2A launched in April 2025 with support and contributions from more than 50 technology partners and major service providers, including Atlassian, Box, Cohere, Intuit, LangChain, MongoDB, PayPal, Salesforce, SAP, ServiceNow, Workday, Accenture, Deloitte, McKinsey, PwC, TCS, and Wipro.

The Linux Foundation announced on April 9, 2026 that A2A had surpassed 150 supporting organizations, had integrations across Google, Microsoft, and AWS platforms, and was seeing production deployments across multiple industries.
A2A is now an open standard hosted by the Linux Foundation after being originally developed by Google.
The current A2A GitHub latest release is v1.0.1, published May 28, 2026; the repository had 24,247 stars and 2,459 forks when checked on June 12, 2026.
Google ADK Python latest release is v2.2.0, published June 4, 2026; the repository had 20,081 stars and 3,554 forks when checked on June 12, 2026.
ADK Python 2.0 adds a graph-based workflow runtime for routing, fan-out/fan-in, loops, retry, state management, dynamic nodes, human-in-the-loop, and nested workflows.
Google announced Python ADK v1.0.0 as a production-ready stable release at Google I/O 2025 and also introduced Java ADK v0.1.0.
A2A v0.2 introduced support for stateless interactions and standardized authentication schemes based on an OpenAPI-like authentication schema.
The ADK documentation currently presents ADK Python 2.0 GA with graph workflows and collaborative agents, plus language tabs for Python, JavaScript, Go, Java, and Kotlin.

The official A2A documentation positions the stack as: build agents with ADK or another framework, equip them with MCP or another tool layer, and communicate with A2A across remote agents, local agents, and humans.

angles: Position ADK and A2A as complementary layers, not competing choices: ADK builds and orchestrates agents; A2A lets those agents interoperate across frameworks, vendors, clouds, and organizations.
Use the three-layer mental model developers search for in 2026: MCP for tool/context access, ADK for agent logic and workflows, A2A for cross-agent communication.
Lead with practical architecture: expose each important ADK agent as an A2A server using Agent Cards, then build an orchestrator that discovers and delegates to remote agents.

Differentiate from shallow explainers by covering what breaks in production: identity, auth, agent-card trust, task lifecycle observability, streaming, retries, and backward-compatible protocol changes.

Address the hype gap honestly: A2A has strong ecosystem momentum and Linux Foundation governance, but teams still need proof-of-concept validation before putting critical workflows on heterogeneous agent meshes.
Use cross-framework examples such as Google ADK with Microsoft Agent Framework, LangGraph, BeeAI, or custom agents to make interoperability concrete.
Explain when not to use A2A: internal sub-agent delegation inside one ADK app may be simpler than exposing networked A2A endpoints.
